title: Symphony No. 1 in D major
hook: Mahler’s first symphony begins with nature waking at dawn and ends in a storm that breaks into triumph.

painting.title: Spring in the Prater
painting.pairingNote: Vienna’s Prater park at the very start of spring, the trees still bare and the light new, painted in the city where Mahler studied; for this symphony’s first movement he once used the title “Spring and no end”.

facts: Mahler wrote the symphony mainly between late 1887 and March 1888 in Leipzig, where he was second conductor at the opera. He was 27, and far better known as a conductor than as a composer.

He borrowed from his own songs. The main theme of the first movement is the tune of “Ging heut’ Morgen übers Feld” (“I walked across the fields this morning”), and the slow movement quotes another song from the same cycle, the *Songs of a Wayfarer*.

The first performance, in Budapest on 20 November 1889, presented it as a “symphonic poem” in two parts, and it was not well received. For Hamburg in 1893 Mahler added a programme and the title *Titan*, after a novel by Jean Paul. Later he dropped the programme, the title and an extra movement, *Blumine*. The four-movement symphony was published in 1899.

The third movement turns the children’s round “Frère Jacques” (in Austria “Bruder Martin”) into a funeral march in the minor. Mahler once titled it a funeral march “in the manner of Callot”, after the French printmaker of grotesque scenes, and the idea behind it is a hunter’s funeral with the animals of the forest following the coffin.
bigPicture.inOneLine: nature waking at dawn and a walk in the fields (I), a stamping country dance (II), a mock funeral (III), a storm that fights its way to victory (IV).

movements.heading: Langsam, schleppend – Immer sehr gemächlich
movements.summary: The symphony opens with a single note, A, held by the strings across seven octaves, the highest violins playing ghostly [[harmonics|harmonics]]. Out of this haze come sounds of nature: a falling two-note call, distant fanfares, a cuckoo. Then the cellos start a cheerful walking tune, borrowed from Mahler’s song about crossing the fields one morning. The movement is a loose [[sonata-form|sonata form]], and at the end it bursts into D major.

mainIdeas.name: The falling call
mainIdeas.description: two notes a fourth apart, first in the woodwinds and later in a clarinet as a cuckoo. It returns in every movement.

mainIdeas.name: The fanfares
mainIdeas.description: military calls, first in the clarinets, then trumpets placed far away.

mainIdeas.name: The walking song
mainIdeas.description: a carefree tune in the cellos, from “Ging heut’ Morgen übers Feld”.

notice: Listen to how long it takes for anything like a tune to arrive. The first three minutes are only a held note and scattered calls, as if the music were waking up.
The two-note falling call is everywhere: in the introduction, in the cuckoo, and as the first two notes of the walking song.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Kubelík recorded the symphony in Munich in 1967, as part of his complete Mahler cycle with the Bavarian Radio Symphony Orchestra for Deutsche Grammophon. On the Spotify album the symphony is tracks 1–4, followed by the *Songs of a Wayfarer* sung by Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau, the cycle the symphony borrows from.

movements.heading: Kräftig bewegt, doch nicht zu schnell
movements.tempo: Kräftig bewegt, doch nicht zu schnell
movements.summary: A robust, stamping country dance, a [[landler|Ländler]], in three beats. The low strings thump out the rhythm, the tune swaggers, the horns whoop. In the middle, the [[trio|trio]] is softer and more graceful, a gentle sway in the strings. Then the stamping dance returns, shorter and louder.

mainIdeas.name: The Ländler
mainIdeas.description: a heavy-footed tune over a thumping bass, with whooping horns and shrill clarinets.

mainIdeas.name: The trio
mainIdeas.description: a slower, swaying melody for the strings, with a touch of Viennese charm.

stops.hear: Low strings thump out a rhythm; the tune enters, sturdy and swinging
The whole orchestra joins; horns whoop, clarinets squeal
The tune returns and the music drives faster and harder
A horn call, then a soft, swaying melody in the strings
The cellos take up a tender, waltz-like tune
The stamping dance returns, louder and fuller

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: A quick rush and a sudden, emphatic end

notice: Listen to the bass under the opening tune. It is built on the same falling interval as the first movement’s call.

movements.heading: Feierlich und gemessen, ohne zu schleppen
movements.tempo: Feierlich und gemessen, ohne zu schleppen
movements.summary: A funeral march made from a nursery round. A timpani taps out two notes, and a solo double bass, high and strained, plays “Bruder Martin” in the minor. The other instruments join one by one, as in a [[canon|canon]]. The procession is interrupted by a village band, vulgar and tearful, and then by a dream: a tender melody from Mahler’s own song about a linden tree. The march returns, and fades away.

mainIdeas.name: The round
mainIdeas.description: “Frère Jacques”, made sad and slow, in the minor.

mainIdeas.name: The band
mainIdeas.description: a cheap, sobbing tune for oboes, clarinets and trumpets, with cymbal and bass drum.

mainIdeas.name: The dream
mainIdeas.description: a soft melody for the strings, from the song “Die zwei blauen Augen” (“The two blue eyes”).

stops.hear: Soft timpani strokes; a single double bass plays “Frère Jacques” in the minor, high and thin
stops.happening: The round as a funeral march, in D minor

stops.hear: A bassoon enters with the same tune, then cellos, tuba and more
stops.happening: The instruments enter one by one: a [[canon|canon]]

stops.hear: Above the procession, an oboe plays a mocking counter-melody
stops.happening: A new line woven on top

stops.hear: Oboes, clarinets and trumpets strike up a sobbing, swaggering tune, with cymbal and bass drum
The mood changes completely: a soft, dreamy melody in the strings
stops.happening: The song “Die zwei blauen Augen”, in G major

stops.hear: The march returns, in a darker key and a little faster; the band joins in

stops.label: Last 40 seconds
stops.hear: The march breaks into fragments; low plucked notes, two at a time, fade out
stops.happening: The procession passes out of sight

notice: The solo double bass is a deliberately odd choice: it plays high in its range, where it sounds thin and uneasy. Mahler wanted a funeral march that is both sad and absurd.
In the dream section the words of the song, which you do not hear, speak of lying under a linden tree, where all was well again.

movements.heading: Stürmisch bewegt
movements.summary: The finale begins with a cymbal crash and a scream from the whole orchestra, straight out of the quiet end of the funeral march. A fierce theme in F minor storms through the brass; a long, tender second theme in the strings offers relief. The struggle goes on, twice reaching for D major, and memories of the first movement return. In the end the brass win through with a [[chorale|chorale]], and the symphony closes in triumph.

mainIdeas.name: The storm theme
mainIdeas.description: a fierce, jagged melody in the brass, in F minor.

mainIdeas.name: The love theme
mainIdeas.description: a broad, warm melody in the violins, in D-flat major.

mainIdeas.name: The chorale
mainIdeas.description: a solemn, hymn-like phrase in the brass, which becomes the symphony’s victory song.

notice: The first move to D major, in the middle of the movement, collapses. Notice how much harder the music has to work to reach it the second time.
In most performances all seven horn players stand up for the final chorale, so that they ring out above the whole orchestra.

threads.title: The falling call
threads.body: The two-note fall of the opening is in the cuckoo, in the walking song, in the Ländler’s bass, in the timpani of the funeral march and in the finale’s themes. It ties the symphony together.

threads.title: Songs inside a symphony
threads.body: Two of Mahler’s *Songs of a Wayfarer* are woven in: the morning walk in the first movement and the linden-tree dream in the third. The words are absent, but the tunes carry their meaning.

threads.title: From dawn to triumph
threads.body: The symphony moves from a held note at first light, through a dance and a mock funeral, to a hard-won victory. Mahler’s discarded programme called the finale “From Hell to Paradise”.
